rationale: The student added 7 + 6 to get 13 and wrote 513 instead of regrouping. A place-value model demonstrating make-a-ten will visually show 10 ones bundling into 1 ten, leaving the remaining ones behind.

script.focus: ten ones bundling together to become one ten in the tens column

intent: Demonstrate make-a-ten on the place-value with values [14]. Tutor points at: ten ones bundling together to become one ten in the tens column

frames.caption: Here are 14 ones. That is too many for the ones place: it can only hold 0 to 9.
Bundle ten of them. Ten ones make one ten, so the bundle moves to the tens place. 4 ones are left.
Write 1 in the tens place and 4 in the ones place: 14. One digit per place.

judgement.reasoning: The student wrote 513 for 37 + 26 because they do not understand that the ones place can only hold a single digit and that 13 ones must be regrouped. The demo directly isolates bundling >9 ones (using 14) into 1 ten and leftover ones, explicitly stating 'That is too many for the ones place: it can only hold 0 to 9' and 'One digit per place.' It is a passive worked demo stepping back to the prerequisite place-value concept, perfectly targeted without leaking the exact problem 37 + 26.
judgement.verdict: Yes, this demo directly targets the misconception that both digits can sit in the ones place by demonstrating bundling 14 ones into 1 ten and 4 ones.
